Ranking Methodology

The Research Oriented Global University Ranking employs a novel dual-component ranking (DCR) methodology applied to 1,764 universities from 89 countries, using the Scopus-powered SciVal platform for the reference window 2021–2025. DCR first divides all institutions into five distinct performance groups using hierarchical clustering, and then, using the Copeland pairwise method, ranks institutions by counting all head-to-head indicator wins across all opponents, thus covering the full resolution spectrum from broad performance tier assignments to precise rank positions.

Component 1 — Clustering. Institutions are stratified into five structurally homogeneous clusters using hierarchical agglomerative clustering with complete linkage on ten log-normalised, max-scaled SciVal indicators. The number of clusters (k = 5) was selected based on two internal indices: the Silhouette score (SS), and the Calinski–Harabasz index (CHI).

Component 2 — Pairwise Ranking. Universities are ranked across the full population using the Copeland pairwise method. Each institution is compared to every other on each of the ten indicators and receives one win per head-to-head victory. The final Copeland Score (0–100) reflects the fraction of all pairwise comparisons won, normalised to the theoretical maximum. No subjective weights are applied at any point.

Comparison with existing rankings (THE and QS). Spearman rank correlation with Times Higher Education 2026 (ρ = 0.835, n = 1,281) and QS World University Rankings 2026 (ρ = 0.661, n = 1,095) confirms strong convergent validity. The THE–QS cross-correlation is ρ = 0.833, indicating this ranking is at least as convergent with established systems as they are with each other.

Table 1. SciVal Indicators Used in the Ranking

10 indicators across 7 research performance dimensions. All metrics are sourced from SciVal (Elsevier), reference window 2021–2025.

# Dimension Metric (SciVal label) Abbrev. Description Rationale
1 Productivity Scholarly Output (articles, reviews, conference papers, books and chapters) SO Indicates the prolificacy of an entity — the number of publications indexed in Scopus. Used as a measure of how active the entity is.
2 Journal quality Publications in Top 10% Journal Percentiles by CiteScore Percentile (%) P10%JP
CiteScore		 The share of an entity's publications appearing in journals ranked in the top 10% by CiteScore Percentile. CiteScore reflects the yearly average citations to a journal over a 4-year window. Captures venue prestige, complementing direct citation counts by reflecting the quality of outlets where researchers choose to publish.
3 Citation impact Field-Weighted Citation Impact — average (excl. self-citations) FWCI
average		 Compares citations received by an entity's publications with the average for all publications of the same year, type, and discipline in Scopus. Adjusts citation counts for the research field. A value > 1 indicates above-world-average citation impact. Enables fair comparison across disciplines.
Field-Weighted Citation Impact — median (excl. self-citations) FWCI
median		 Same field-normalisation as FWCI average, but uses the median across the portfolio instead of the mean. Average FWCI is highly sensitive to outliers. Median FWCI is a complementary metric; the world median is approximately 0.4 per year, versus 1.0 for the world mean.
Output in Top 10% Citation Percentiles, field-weighted (%) O10%CP The percentage of publications falling in the top 10% most-cited globally, after field and year normalisation. Rewards institutions whose work achieves exceptional citation impact (top decile globally), providing a high-excellence threshold measure.
4 Viewed impact Field-Weighted Views Impact FWVI Compares abstract views and full-text clicks received by an entity's publications with the average for similar publications. Views data sourced from Scopus usage logs. A field-normalised measure of online readership that captures research reach beyond the formal citation network, including audiences who read but do not publish.
Output in Top 10% Views Percentiles, field-weighted (%) O10%VP The percentage of publications falling in the top 10% most-viewed globally, after field normalisation. Rewards institutions whose work attracts the broadest readership, complementing citation-based excellence measures.
5 Collaboration International Collaboration (%) IC The percentage of an entity's publications that have at least one co-author from a different country. Measures how often an entity collaborates internationally. International co-authorship is associated with higher visibility and citation impact.
6 Patenting Patent Citations PC The total count of citations received by an entity's publications within patent documents. Captures the uptake of university research by inventors and industry, reflecting the applied and commercially relevant dimension of scientific output.
7 Policy impact Scholarly Output cited by Policy (%) SOCP The percentage of an entity's publications that have been cited in policy documents indexed in SciVal. Measures the share of an institution's output that informs real-world policy decisions, extending research impact beyond the academic citation network.
Alexey Remizov 1
Alexey Remizov completed his Ph.D. at Nazarbayev University in 2024, where his research was primarily focused on climate-related challenges, particularly climate zoning and energy efficiency in the built environment. While climate remains his core research domain, Alexey has recently expanded his academic interests to include the assessment of scientific performance and research impact. Under the guidance of Dr. Shazim Ali Memon, he is currently investigating novel methodologies for fair and comprehensive evaluation of researcher productivity, emphasising multidimensional bibliometric analysis and performance-based ranking systems.

Methodology & Authors

Ranking Methodology

The Research Oriented Global University Ranking applies a two-stage bibliometric framework to 1,764 universities from 89 countries, drawing on the Scopus-powered SciVal platform for the five-year reference window 2021–2025.

In Stage 1, institutions are stratified into five structurally homogeneous clusters using hierarchical agglomerative clustering with complete linkage on ten log-normalised, max-scaled SciVal indicators. The number of clusters (k = 5) was selected by balancing statistical validity criteria (silhouette coefficient, Calinski–Harabasz index, Davies–Bouldin index) against interpretability: k = 3 was statistically optimal but too coarse; k = 7 and k = 10 produced degenerate clusters of fewer than 15 institutions. In Stage 2, universities are ranked within the full population using the Copeland pairwise method: each institution is compared to every other on each of the ten indicators and receives one win per head-to-head victory. The final Copeland Score (0–100) reflects the fraction of all pairwise comparisons won. No subjective weights are applied at any stage.

Stage 1 · Clustering

Hierarchical complete-linkage clustering (k = 5) on 10 log / max-normalised SciVal indicators partitions 1,764 universities into five structurally distinct research profiles.

Stage 2 · Pairwise Ranking

Copeland's method compares every pair of institutions on each indicator. The Copeland Score equals the fraction of all pairwise comparisons won, requiring no subjective weights.

Validation

Spearman rank correlation with Times Higher Education 2026 (ρ = 0.835, n = 1,281) and QS 2026 (ρ = 0.661, n = 1,095) confirms strong convergent validity while maintaining complementary coverage.

Indicators used (SciVal, 2021–2025): Scholarly Output · Publications in Top 10% Journal Percentiles by CiteScore (%) · Field-Weighted Citation Impact (average & median) · Output in Top 10% Citation Percentiles (field-weighted, %) · Field-Weighted Views Impact · Output in Top 10% Views Percentiles (field-weighted, %) · International Collaboration (%) · Patent Citations · Scholarly Output cited by Policies (%).
